focus: Section 2.1.1 (Description of PageRank Calculation). Explain how PageRank distributes each page's rank equally over its outgoing links, mixed with a damping factor d. Use a tiny web of 4 pages whose links the learner can toggle, plus a slider for d and for the number of iterations. Show the link matrix, the rank vector after each iteration and the final ranks. Guide the learner through a symmetric cycle (all ranks equal) and a page that many others link to. Include the random-surfer interpretation and the limitation of pages with no outgoing links. Check that, with the normalized form, ranks stay non-negative and sum to one.
audience: engineering undergraduate who knows matrices and basic probability
excerpt: 2.1.1 Description of PageRank Calculation (paraphrased). We assume page A has pages T1...Tn which point to it (i.e., are citations). The parameter d is a damping factor which can be set between 0 and 1. We usually set d to 0.85. Also C(A) is defined as the number of links going out of page A. The PageRank of a page A is given as follows: PR(A) = (1 - d) + d (PR(T1)/C(T1) + ... + PR(Tn)/C(Tn)). Note that the PageRanks form a probability distribution over web pages, so the sum of all web pages' PageRanks will be one. PageRank or PR(A) can be calculated using a simple iterative algorithm, and corresponds to the principal eigenvector of the normalized link matrix of the web. 2.1.2 Intuitive Justification: PageRank can be thought of as a model of user behavior. We assume there is a random surfer who is given a web page at random and keeps clicking on links, never hitting back but eventually gets bored and starts on another random page. The probability that the random surfer visits a page is its PageRank. And, the d damping factor is the probability at each page the random surfer will get bored and request another random page.
